A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SURGE benchmark and study. Text, figures, tables and equations are readable throughout. v3 ends with references; v4 includes Appendices A–D, although C.8 contains only an FL placeholder. The supplied material supports reliable comparison.

before.justification: v3 reports original evaluations of 21 LLMs under three prompting settings, error analyses and formal-language training experiments.

after.justification: v4 retains those empirical results and adds qualitative case analyses in Sections 4.3 and 5.5.

M1.justification: The four benchmark-construction approaches, LLM execution-prediction framework and formal-language fine-tuning approach are retained. Expanded sanitization and implementation descriptions do not establish a changed algorithm, architecture or training objective.

E1.justification: Both versions retain eight subsets and 1,160 problems. However, v4 Section 3.2 still lists CL languages as C++, Java and JavaScript, matching v3, while Appendix C.2 and Table 7 specify Python, C++ and JavaScript. Whether this reflects changed coverage or inconsistent documentation is unresolved. Other appendix descriptions elaborate retained subsets.

E2.justification: All 21 evaluated models remain in v4 Appendix A, Table 5. The ten-model selection in v4 Table 2 does not remove comparators from the full evaluation. Comparator membership in the retained scaling, runtime and error analyses also remains unchanged.

E3.justification: Reported few-shot settings differ: v3 Table 1 specifies three examples for both RL and DR, whereas v4 Appendix C.3.1 specifies one for its RL prompt and C.7.1 specifies six for DR. These are limited reported protocol changes; the PDFs do not establish reruns. The three prompting regimes and temperature-zero decoding remain.

E4.justification: New Sections 4.3 and 5.5 add case analyses of larger-model failures, LLaMA zero-shot failures, C++ bit-field reasoning, state tracing and TSP prediction difficulties. These provide a limited qualitative extension to the retained language, difficulty, runtime, compiler, error-type and scaling analyses.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, evaluation seeds, confidence intervals or significance tests. The added dataset-frequency tables and standard metric formulas do not introduce uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: All 1,008 numerical entries in v3 Table 2 match v4 Table 5; Tables 3–4 also retain their values. Figure 1 changes the repository-level points for GPT-4o-mini and LLaMA-3.1-8B from zero to positive plotted values. Sections 4.3 and 5.5 additionally report qualitative observations about reasoning failures and computational boundaries.

T1.justification: No substantive theoretical assumptions, proofs or mathematical reasoning are added or revised. The FL scoring formula is retained. Appendix equations specify standard scientific-computing tasks and explain existing metrics, including RAE, exact matching and rank correlation.

C1.justification: The central contributions remain the eight-subset SURGE benchmark, evaluation of 21 LLMs and empirical scaling study. Abstract, introduction and conclusion revisions preserve the claims about surrogate-execution potential and substantial remaining limitations.

C2.justification: v4 substantially expands interpretation through explanations of overthinking, proof-error misclassification, semantic reasoning, state tracing and combinatorial limits. Its new Limitations section identifies excluded hardware-dependent and real-time environments, resource constraints and the gap between controlled evaluation and dynamic software development. v3's speculative suggestion that Claude and GPT share a similar way of thinking is removed.

D1.justification: Appendices B–D add refactoring and evaluation prompts, code examples, dataset breakdowns, numerical algorithms, output-alignment rules and fine-tuning settings. Table 12 newly specifies Llama-Factory-related training details, including learning rate, epochs, scheduler, warmup and precision. Section 3.1 expands sanitization documentation. However, v3's 260K-proof training-data count disappears, and FL appendix details remain a placeholder.

R1.justification: v4 removes the broad survey of multilingual, competition, data-science, repository and reasoning benchmarks, including CRUXEval, SWE-bench, RepoBench and DS-1000. This substantially contracts the benchmark-positioning discussion. It adds Schäfer et al. on unit-test generation and Zheng et al. on LlamaFactory while retaining the central surrogate-model positioning.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, dataset descriptions, metric explanations and conclusion are extensively condensed or rewritten. New anomaly, model-behavior and limitations sections, together with structured technical appendices, substantially reorganize the exposition.

P2.justification: The full results table moves to Appendix A, with a ten-model main-text version and blue cell shading. Table 1 loses its example-count column; Tables 6–12 and extensive formatted prompt/code listings are added. Figures 1 and 5 are revised visually, and tables, captions and surrounding text are substantially rearranged.

improvement.justification: v4 makes the benchmark easier to inspect through concrete prompts, code examples and fine-tuning settings, while new case analyses and explicit applicability limits improve qualification of its claims. These provide a limited net gain. Conflicting CL language descriptions, unexplained few-shot-count changes, the unfinished FL appendix, removal of the 260K training-data count and reduced benchmark-related work prevent a substantial improvement in reproducibility and positioning.
